newsitem.title: UK: CWS sacks executives, mounts action on predator.
newsitem.headline: CWS sacks executives, mounts action on predator.

text.p: Britain's mutually-owned Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) has sacked two senior executives with links with entreprenur Andrew Regan whose 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) hostile bid for CWS collapsed last week, newspapers said on Monday.

The Financial Times newspaper said CWS dismissed manager Alan Green, controller of CWS retailing business and chief general manager for buying, markets and supply chain David Chambers during the weekend after accusing them of plotting with Regan to launch the hostile bid.
Both executives were suspended on April 18 for serious breach of trust.
Green had admitted in a High Court affidavit last week that he had passed confidential information to Regan and his specially-formed bidding vehicle Galileo.

The Independent newspaper said CWS had also written to the London Stock Exchange seeking an immediate enquiry into the possibility of insider trading in the shares of Regan's listed company Lanica Trust.
Lanica's shares were suspended in February after they soared to 1,950 pence from under 200p per share last autumn, despite its comments that it was unaware of any reasons behind the rise.
The paper said CWS also intensified its attack on the failed predator by writing to UK's Department of Trade and Industry and the Bank of England to look into the matter.
Earlier, on Friday, the Manchester-based supermarkets to funeral parlours group reiterated that it was not for sale and would continue to provide service to ordinary Britons.
"The CWS is not for sale to Mr Regan or to anyone else. The CWS has a strong future serving everyday needs of ordinary people," CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth said on Friday.

CWS has already initiated a private prosecution against Regan and his business associate David Lyons as well as action accusing Green of theft. A preliminary hearing is due to take place in the City of London magistrates court on May 28.
